news_drafts.headline: North Lanarkshire's housing revenue account gap for 2027/28 falls to £4.253m from £7.484m
news_drafts.lead:
North Lanarkshire Council's housing revenue account, the separate ring-fenced account for its own housing stock, paid for by rents, now has a budget gap of £4.253m for 2027/28. The medium-term financial plan presented in August 2026 put the gap at £7.484m. Revised planning assumptions reduced it by £3.231m, according to the paper going to the Housing Committee on 4 November 2026.

The paper sets cost pressures of £7.581m against base budget reductions of £3.328m, which leaves the £4.253m gap. It says the gap is to be reviewed at the December 2026 Council meeting, when estimates and rent levels for 2027/28 are to be approved.

Appendix 2 gives revised gaps for later years. For 2028/29 the gap is £9.751m, against £9.813m in the medium-term plan. For 2029/30 it is £13.998m, against £12.590m. The paper says unbudgeted pressures will be managed where possible through in-year action or unallocated reserves, with recurring impacts addressed in future medium-term financial plans.

news_drafts.headline: North Lanarkshire health and social care board plan sets out £67.464m budget gap over three years
news_drafts.lead:
North Lanarkshire's Integration Joint Board (IJB), which oversees health and social care services delegated to it, has a medium-term financial plan (its plan for the next three years, showing the gap between what it expects to spend and what it expects to have). The plan identified a cumulative budget gap of £67.464m over the three years, including £23.923m in 2026/27. The approved budget for 2026/27 is £915.495m, and a recurring savings programme of £22.727m is measured against that year's gap.

The 2026/27 financial monitoring report shows social care services delegated to the partnership projecting an overspend of £4.872m before employee costs. Most of it relates to payments to other bodies, mainly care at home and independent care home places. Budgets were increased by £23.155m for inflation and expected demand, before a £7.900m savings requirement was applied. The paper links the overspend to demand, cost pressures and a shortfall against planned savings.

A separate reserves update, at period 6 (11 September 2026), gives a projected social care overspend of £1.647m. It assumes that sum will be funded from the Risk Reserve, money the board has set aside. It forecasts £5.008m of reserves used for social care. The board's governance progress paper says it approved a savings programme in March 2026 to meet the budget gap and that work on it is "well underway". It gives no savings amount.

news_drafts.headline: North Lanarkshire holds £368m in reserves despite £75.5m three-year budget gap.
news_drafts.lead: North Lanarkshire Council faces a structural budget gap (the shortfall between planned spending and expected income) of £75.5 million over three years to 2029/30, down from £85.9 million the year before. However, the council's usable reserves (money set aside for specific purposes or emergencies) increased to £368.3 million in 2025/26, from £346.3 million the previous year. Auditors have flagged this tension directly: the Accounts Commission states the council should "reassess the purpose and scale of its reserves held in order to address the budget gap". The council underspent its 2025/26 budget by £7 million and achieved most of its planned savings, but auditors warn that "the scope for further savings is narrowing" and future reductions will require "more difficult decisions".

findings.headline: Over £5m in grants were distributed to owners between 2020 and 2024, most of it for mandatory disabled adaptations.
findings.detail: The paper says the council engaged with thousands of owners through pro-active visits over the period. It also reports an average of 3,000 housing adaptations a year across all tenures.
findings.matters: Mandatory adaptation grants are a demand-led spend that councils and lenders can benchmark, since the volume depends on the age profile and disability levels of the local population.

findings.headline: The Housing (Scotland) Act 2025 introduces new homelessness prevention duties, including an 'Ask and Act' duty on relevant public bodies.
findings.detail: The paper says the duty will require relevant public bodies to identify people at risk of homelessness and take action to prevent it. It describes this as a significant shift in practice for health and social care services. The paper does not give a cost for the new duties.
findings.matters: A new statutory duty that moves work onto health and social care services may create costs for partner bodies, which finance officers at councils and IJBs will need to plan for.

findings.headline: Housing invests more than £1.2 million per year in commissioned housing support services, which the paper says are currently funded primarily through Housing resources.
findings.detail: The paper says these services cover homelessness prevention, tenancy sustainment and independent living support. It calls for aligned commissioning and shared investment across housing, health and social care.
findings.matters: Funding that sits mainly in the housing budget but serves health and social care outcomes is a cost-sharing question that finance directors in other councils and IJBs also face.
findings.figures: more than £1.2 million per annum in commissioned housing support services
findings.quote: Whilst these services are currently funded primarily through Housing resources

findings.headline: Repeat homelessness in North Lanarkshire fell 6% in 2025/26, while it rose 5% nationally.
findings.detail: The paper links the local fall to tenancy sustainment, housing support and homelessness prevention activity. It also reports that homelessness applications fell by 2% in the year.
findings.matters: A divergence from the national trend in repeat presentations is a demand signal that councils with similar homelessness services can compare against their own figures.
findings.figures: repeat homelessness down 6% locally; up 5% nationally; homelessness applications down 2% (2,188 in 2024/25 to 2,135 in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Repeat homelessness reduced by 6%, compared with a 5% increase nationally.

findings.headline: Children in temporary accommodation in North Lanarkshire fell from 220 to 165 (25%) in 2025/26, while the Scottish figure rose from 10,180 to 10,715 (5%).
findings.detail: The paper reports a fall in households with children or a pregnant woman in temporary accommodation, from 125 to 90 (28%). It contrasts both measures with national increases.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a measure a finance officer can compare directly across councils facing the same homelessness pressures.
findings.figures: 220 children to 165 children (25%) at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026; Scotland 10,180 to 10,715 children (5%); households with children or a pregnant woman 125 to 90 (28%)
findings.quote: The number of children in temporary accommodation reduced from 220 to 165 (25%) during 2025/26.

daily_post.headline: Legal and Estates will consider clawback, pre-emption or equivalent mechanisms to protect public value on a disposal below market value.
daily_post.lead: Clawback terms determine whether the council could recover some value if the land is later sold or changes use, which matters to any reader assessing the transaction's long-term financial effect.
